patches.new:
The ELM predicts that when motivation or ability to process is low (e.g., distracted, disinterested, or cognitively overloaded), peripheral cues dominate.

This produces a counter-intuitive result worth knowing: **mild distraction can increase persuasion**. Festinger and Maccoby (1964) found that an audience distracted during a counter-attitudinal message was *more* persuaded than an attentive one. The reason is that the distraction interferes with **counterarguing** — the silent rebuttals a listener would otherwise generate — leaving peripheral cues such as the speaker's likability free to do the work. Petty and colleagues later generalised the finding: distraction disrupts whatever the *dominant* cognitive response would have been, so it increases persuasion when the audience would have argued back (weak arguments, or a message they oppose) and **decreases** it when the audience would have been generating favourable thoughts (strong arguments they already lean toward).

sources.title: Petty, Wells & Brock, “Distraction can enhance or reduce yielding to propaganda” — reports Festinger and Maccoby's 1964 distraction finding and generalises it to disruption of the dominant cognitive response

visual.title: The gate, the dissonance, and the prediction
visual.alt: A persuasive message passing through a gate asking whether the listener is both motivated and able to think about it, branching to a central route producing durable change that predicts behaviour and a peripheral route producing fragile change; a panel showing a dissonant pair of cognitions with the three resolutions and the insufficient justification, post-decision and effort justification paradigms; and a panel of the conditions under which an attitude predicts behaviour, ending with the three components of the theory of planned behaviour feeding intention.
visual.caption: Both motivation and ability are needed for the central route; losing either sends the message down the peripheral one, where the change will not last.
